title: Beyond Mutations: Pathogenic DNA Repeats as Regulators of the Lung Cancer Epigenome
content: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer mortality despite advances in genomic profiling and targeted therapy. Although epidermal growth factor receptor, KRAS proto-oncogene GTPase, tumor protein p53, serine/threonine kinase 11, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1, and ALK receptor tyrosine kinase alterations guide precision oncology, they do not fully explain tumor epigenetic heterogeneity and plasticity. Repetitive DNA—including satellite DNA, microsatellites, telomeres, ribosomal DNA, transposable elements, and expanded nucleotide repeats—actively regulates DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin looping, noncoding RNA production, R-loop formation, and 3-dimensional genome organization. Repeat dysregulation promotes genome instability, transcriptional reprogramming, immune modulation, metabolic adaptation, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, stemness, ferroptosis resistance, and therapeutic escape. Repeat-derived RNAs can recruit chromatin modifiers, sequester RNA-binding proteins, and remodel enhancers and activate innate immune pathways. Because many repeat-associated epigenetic alterations are reversible, they offer opportunities for intervention using epigenetic drugs; clustered, regularly interspaced, short palindromic repeats-based regulation; antisense oligonucleotides; RNA interference; and synthetic-lethality strategies. In this review we examine pathogenic DNA repeats as regulators of the lung cancer epigenome and therapeutic targets beyond mutation-centered precision oncology.
